en: HSS10 NSUG Xc 14/39, 114r3–123r7, corresponding to Toh. 1264: Oṃ namaḥ śrīhevajrāya ||
I bow to the glorious He-ka-ra-vajra, the state of supreme bliss, whose singular form is free from conceptual construction;
who arises from merit and wisdom; whose nature is all things, both moving and unmoving, without exception;
who is awakened by all joys; who is supremely stainless; the Lord of the *ḍākinī* circle.
Having bowed to that [deity] with all my being, I shall explain its sādhana, whose words are clear and lucid.
Having bowed to the lotus feet of the true guru, for the sake of my own remembrance, I shall [recount] that which was properly heard from him— the tradition that is exceedingly difficult to obtain.

Moreover, having beheld the realm of sentient beings despondent due to the fear of falling into the great abyss of saṃsāra— which is difficult to cross and most terrible— the yogi, overwhelmed by the penetration of the flavor of exceedingly weighty compassion, having mastered the means for crossing the ocean of saṃsāra, being free from all faults such as contempt for his guru, endowed with virtues such as generosity, having conquered his senses, observing the commitments (*samaya*) of the five nectars and so forth, and having been consecrated in the maṇḍala taught in the *Śrī Hevajra* and properly authorized, rises early in the morning at a certain place conducive to the mind, such as a cremation ground, where the ground has been purified with the sun, moon, water, perfumes, and special medicinal herbs.
First, one should meditate upon the deceased as having the very nature of the *dharmadhātu*.
Standing at his chest, one should meditate upon the supreme state.
Seated in the vajra-paryaṅka posture, with hands restrained in the *dhyāna-mudrā*, [one should practice].
One should visualize the syllable *repha* within one's own heart, which becomes a solar disc;
and right there, one should also visualize the syllable *hūṃ*, whose nature is wisdom and means.
From the syllable *hūṃ*, a black and most terrible vajra arises.
One should meditate on the reality of *hūṃ* situated within the hub of that vajra. Again, having seen it transformed from the syllable *hūṃ*, one should visualize oneself as the embodiment of Hatred.
The great black Vajra-janma, resembling a blue lotus—
according to the oral instructions, there are three types of the form of the deity to be visualized;
from among these three, the yogi should perform the meditation according to his own inclination.
One should indeed meditate with faith upon the Great Radiant Solitary Hero.

Then, having placed one's own seed-syllable upon the sun in the heart, and having visualized the Blessed One in his manifest form together with his retinue drawn toward oneself from the sky by its rays, one should worship him in due order with the eight goddesses beginning with Gaurī—whose sprout-like hands shine with various special offerings and who possess the mantras *rakṣa rakṣa mala vimala*—and with the specific offerings of external worship.

There, Gaurī holds the moon; Caurī, the sun; Vettālī, water; Ghasmarī, strength; Pukkasī, fragrance; Śavarī, taste; Caṇḍālī plays the hand-drum (ḍamaruka); and Ḍombī displays the gesture of embracing.
Then, right here in the presence of the Blessed One, one should perform the confession of sins produced by beginningless habitual tendencies and so forth:
"I confess every sin of my own—whether committed, caused to be committed, or approved.
I rejoice in all the roots of virtue belonging to all Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and ordinary beings."

Whatever merit I have acquired for myself, I dedicate it all toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment. From this moment until the end of awakening, I go for refuge to the Buddha; I go for refuge to the Dharma, which is the nature of the intrinsic being of all phenomena, whose form is great bliss, the He-ka-ra vajra, and which is taught as having the nature of both the generation and completion stages.
"I go for refuge to the Saṅgha, that host of Ḍākinīs stationed upon the wheel.

These sentient beings, submerged in the ocean of saṃsāra, shall be uplifted by me—in the form of Śrī Heruka—through the bestowing of the lamp of the teaching of the Dharma of the Vajra Way, and they shall be established in the characteristic of the Mahāmudrā-siddhi, which consists of the mass of supreme non-dual bliss that is like an illusion. Thus one should generate the mind of awakening (*bodhicitta*). This very Heruka-yoga is the unsurpassed among all yogas, characterized as the most excellent, the peerless supreme means for achieving Buddhahood; "I have taken refuge in it."

Then, one should cultivate great loving-kindness (*mahāmaitrī*), characterized by the love for all sentient beings as if they were an only son; great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), characterized by the desire to deliver them from suffering and the causes of suffering; great sympathetic joy (*mahāmuditā*), characterized by the manifestation of great joy toward all sentient beings; and great equanimity (*mahopekṣā*), characterized by indifference toward all constructed objects and the like.

Then, having mentally apprehended that all phenomena are constructed by the mind, one should realize: "This very mind, being deluded, appears in various forms. Just as in the delusion caused by grief and so forth, there exists no object of perception (*grāhya*) other than the mind; and because of the absence of an object, that mind does not exist as a subject (*grāhaka*) either. Therefore, knowing that this entire universe consists of mind, and strengthening that very realization, one should recite the mantra which encapsulates the essential reality of all things without exception, in order to abandon ordinary ego-clinging: *oṃ śūnyatājñānavajrasvabhāvātmako ’ham* (I am of the nature of the diamond of the wisdom of emptiness)."

Then, bringing the meaning of the mantra to mind, one should perceive the entire world as being without intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), like the perception of dreams and so forth; characterized by the absence of all [inherent] forms, it is like an illusion and like the stainless midday sky in autumn—this indeed is the Blessed Lady Nairātmyā.

Now, recollecting his vow, he should meditate upon a protective wheel possessing form, which is the natural outflow [of that vow] and has the nature of pure mundane consciousness. He should contemplate a solar disc arising from the syllable *raṃ*, seated upon a universal lotus throne in front of him, wherein is the syllable *hūṃ* of black color and terrifying appearance.
From that arises the universal vajra, five-colored and three-pointed;
within its center, one should again place a sun disk and upon it the syllable *hūṃ*.
From that [arises] the wrathful deity with a downward-pointing trident, unbearable like the fire of cosmic destruction.
With the left hand, the fist with the index finger extended, one should conquer the mandala of Māra;
with the right hand, its face filled with the blazing vajra and the syllable HŪṂ,
the hero is clothed in a tiger-skin garment and adorned with the five mudrās.
Dark-complexioned and most fierce, he inspires extreme terror through fear;
with a garland of heads from which blood drips, he quivers, terrifying and formidable;
his tawny hair blazes upward, and his flickering tongue licks his enemies.
Endowed with three eyes, possessing fangs and a terrifying countenance,
the knower of yoga should cause the mass of his wrath to expand in all directions and intermediate points,
and should pin it down with his own emblem using this mantra.

Oṃ rakṣa rakṣa hūṃ 3 phaṭ svāhā. Until one’s desire is fulfilled, one should contemplate that within [the maṇḍala], the rays of the sun and the viśvavajra—resembling the fire of universal destruction—become one and radiate in every direction, forming a boundary-binding (*sīmābandha*), a vajra-fence (*vajraprākāra*), and above, a vajra-canopy (*vajrapañjara*). Below, through their transformation, one should contemplate the ground made of vajra extending down to the subterranean realm (*ārasātala*).

In its center, one should visualize the form of the *dharmodayā* (source of phenomena), transformed from the syllable *hūṃ*, having the appearance of the rays of the autumnal moon, possessing the nature of Mahāvajradhara, and emitting a multitude of various and wonderful rays; it is triangular, narrow at the bottom and wide at the top, empty within, and contains a universal lotus (*viśvakamala*) with a universal vajra (*viśvavajra*) placed upon its pericarp. At its navel, one should visualize, one above the other, the four great elements, which have the nature of the four maṇḍalas, appear in various forms, and possess the nature of the four goddesses beginning with Pukkasī.

Therein, first, by means of the syllable *yaṃ*, there is a blue wind mandala in the shape of a half-moon, marked with two fluttering banners at its tips. By means of the syllable *raṃ*, there is a red fire mandala, triangular with upward-pointing flames, marked with red tongues of flame. Above that, by means of the syllable *vaṃ*, there is a white, circular water mandala, marked with a vase. Then, by means of the syllable *laṃ*, there is a yellow earth mandala, square, marked with three-pronged vajras at its corners.
Upon that, one should superimpose consciousness as being like an illusion.

Upon that center of the universal vajra, one should meditate on a peaked pavilion (kūṭāgāra) which is the transformation of the four great elements, a condensed and purified buddha-field, pure with the thirty-seven factors conducive to enlightenment, having the nature of Mahāvairocana, variegated with various jewels, and surrounded by eight cremation grounds that indicate the world-systems as infinite, boundless, and like an illusion. It is square, with four gates, adorned with eight pillars,
decorated with four divine railings, and embellished with four archways.
Beautiful with necklaces, half-necklaces, mirrors, flower garlands, canopies, and chowries;
adorned with diamond threads; graced by the splendor of a shimmering multitude of Buddhas;
with the tips of its beautiful banners fluttering; and making the quarters of the sky resound with the ringing of bells.
Gladdened by the five strands of sensual pleasure and by perfect offerings,
that universal eight-petalled lotus in the center possesses filaments;
likewise, there are lotuses in the cardinal and intermediate directions, and seats upon the pericarp.
Brahmā, Indra, Upendra, Rudra, Yama, the Lord of Yakṣas, Nairṛti,
and Vemacitrin provide the seats for Gaurī and the others;
they are positioned facing upward to the south and north, with the four Māras in the center.
One should arrange them according to their respective colors and shapes.
Upon the heart of all the Māras, there is a solar disc;
by means of that, they become terrified and agitated, intent on seeking protection.

Therein, upon the middle seat, by means of the letters beginning with *a* doubled in both direct and reverse order—which indicate the thirty-two marks of a Great Man—there is the moon mandala, whose intrinsic nature is the mirror-like wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*). Above that, by means of the letters beginning with *kṣa* and *ka*, together with *ṭa*, *ḍa*, *da*, *dha*, *bha*, *la*, and *sa*, doubled in both direct and reverse order—which indicate the eighty minor marks—there is the sun mandala, whose intrinsic nature is the wisdom of equality (*samatājñāna*).

Between those two, one should contemplate the two seed-syllables *hūṃ* and *aṃ*; from their transformation, there arise two seeds placed upon one’s own seat, which become a double-bladed vajra and a curved knife joined together and resting within a skull-cup, having the nature of the wisdom of discerning awareness (*pratyavekṣaṇājñāna*).

From the mouths of the rays of light emanating from them, hosts of supreme sages in the form of Ḍākinīs behold the infinite world-realms; having brought the sentient beings therein to full enlightenment, they return and merge with the beings as the wisdom of all-accomplishing action (*kṛtyānuṣṭhānajñāna*).

Then, one should meditate upon the causal Lord Mahāvajrasattva, who is produced from the seed-syllables marked by the signs of the moon and sun; who is composed of an assembly of peerless Jinas as subtle as atoms; who consists of great bliss; who is characterized by the arms, faces, colors, and forms to be described hereafter; and likewise, whose neck is embraced by Nairātmyā, and whose intrinsic nature is the perfectly pure Dharmadhātu.
By this, the fivefold awakening is explained.

By means of the streams of light rays from his heart, one should draw in the entire assembly of Tathāgatas who have assumed the form of Heruka, cause them to enter, and melt them; then, emanate the host of Ḍākinīs beginning with Gaurī, produced from the eight seed-syllables beginning with *Ū*. This is for the purpose of recollection.

Then, having perceived in the sky a subtle Gandharva-being in the form of a mandala, red in color and encircled by two rows of red *hoḥ* syllables, the Vajra-holder—having drawn it in with rays from his heart and caused it to enter, and having placed it in its proper position according to the guru’s instruction—should remain as one whose sole intent is great bliss, having become liquefied through intense passion together with the consort, like the melting of the stainless autumn moon.

Then the four goddesses, Pukkasī and the others, having arrived with great longing and established themselves in their respective directions, rouse the Blessed One with vajra-songs that awaken the mind.
"Arise, O Bharata! Piteously you cry out to me, 'Protect me!
Abandon me, O Desire, for the sake of the great union of bliss; [abandon] this void-meditation!"
"O brother-in-law, shake off [this state]; I am dying! Get up, O Vajra!
Abandon this nature of desolation; O Śavarī, may the task be accomplished!"
O Lord of the Gods, having invited me, why do you remain in solitude?
I am a Caṇḍālī; without you, I cannot even be seen.
O Indīālī, arise! I know that you are indeed yourself.
We are but low-born Dombīs; do not, do not inflict such a cruel wound of compassion upon us.

Then, in accordance with the song, like one awakened from sleep, one should visualize that pair of seed-syllables produced from the withdrawal of the moon's liquid, the pair of signs transformed from them, and those very two seed-syllables placed within the sun and moon in their center, which have the nature of the omniscient gnosis.

Therefore, having emanated the Tathāgatas in the form of ḍākinīs through the yoga of radiation, and perceiving all of that as being like an illusion, like a dream, and dependent upon one's own mind through the yoga of reabsorption, one should meditate on oneself in the form of Śrī Heruka, born from the transformation of the seed-syllables marked by the moon and sun, in union with Nairātmyā.

He tramples the earth with his feet, threatening the gods and asuras; his round red eyes roll in anger, and he is possessed of lovely youth. He has four legs, eight faces, and is adorned with sixteen arms. He stands upon the sun, extremely terrifying, treading upon the four Māras—Kāyamāra, Kleśamāra, Mṛtyumāra, and Devaputramāra. He performs a *tāṇḍava* dance in the half-lotus posture (*ardhaparyaṅka*), wears a garland of fifty human heads from which blood drips, and holds a double-vajra (*viśvavajra*) on his head. His radiance blazes like the fire of universal destruction, and his mouth is expanded by the syllable *HŪṂ*.

His neck is smeared with ashes; his body, face, and the base [of his form] are like a sapphire cloud at the time of universal dissolution; his right and left faces resemble the newly risen autumnal moon and the rays of the sun; his upper face is smoke-colored, formidable, and resembles the body of a bee; his remaining four faces are terrifying with protruding fangs, and each face is adorned with three eyes.

Adorned with five severed heads upon his forehead, frowning with knitted brows, and possessing tawny hair blazing upward, he is naked, endowed with the nine dramatic sentiments, and decorated with the five mudrās:
the bracelet, the earring, the necklace, the armlet, and the girdle.

One-eyedness, asthma, insanity, consumption, leprosy, scabies, jaundice, and enlargement of the spleen; likewise, elephants, horses, donkeys, cows, camels, humans, and *śarabhas*—these are to be known as the two-legged and four-legged beings, respectively, in the eight southern skull-bowls. Earth, wind, fire, moon, sun, Varuṇa, Yama, and Kubera are in the eight northern skull-bowls.

The goddess Nairātmikā is adorned with two arms; her hands hold a skull-cup filled with the blood of the four Māras. With her right hand, she brandishes a sword for cutting through the afflictions (*kleśa*). Her hair is tawny and blazing, her complexion is black, and she is naked. She is embraced by the neck of the Blessed One, adorned with three eyes, standing in the *pratyālīḍha* posture, and decorated with the five mudrās. Above her forehead, she is graced by a row of dry human heads, and she is adorned with a garland of headless trunks; she is the accomplished Ḍākinī.

Then, one should visualize the syllable *HŪṂ* upon the sun situated in the heart-lotus of the Bhagavān, and the syllable *AṂ* upon the moon situated in the heart-lotus of the Bhagavatī. Upon the lotuses of the eyes, ears, nose, tongue, body, and mind, and upon the moon-maṇḍala at the heart where the vital breath has gone, [one sees] the syllables *ĀṂ AṂ IṂ ĪṂ OṂ AṂ*. From these seed-syllables arise the Vajra-Ḍākinīs, marked with their respective signs and enclosed within the union of a sword and a moon. They are white, black, yellow, red, green, and black in color;

they have the nature of Nairātmya-Ḍākinī—namely, delusion, hatred, greed, passion, and envy—and they hold a curved knife (*kartti*) and a skull-cup (*kapāla*). They should be meditated upon as seated in the half-lotus posture (*ardhaparyaṅka*).
These five ḍākinīs, beginning with Vajra, are to be contemplated respectively within the aggregates of form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.

Likewise, among delusion, greed, passion, envy, and hatred, and among the objects of form and so forth, there are Gaurī, Caurī, Vetālī, Ghasmarī, Bhūcarī, and Khecarī; and among the elements of earth, water, fire, and air, there are Pukkasi, Śabarī, Caṇḍālī, and Ḍombī.

Within the lotuses of body, speech, and mind, upon a moon mandala at the heart of the slain life-force (*prāṇa*), there reside the Yoginīs Bhūcarī, Khecarī, and Nairātmyā, born from the seed-syllables Oṃ, Aṃ, and Aṃ, white, red, and black in color respectively; they are fully manifested and stationed according to their respective forms, like the [deities of the] Vajra[-family] and so forth.
Pukkasī is said to be in the flesh, Śavarī is conceived in the blood, Caṇḍālī is said to be in the semen, and Ḍombinī in the marrow and fat.
By this much alone is there the purification of the deity.
Now, another purification should be undertaken with resolute conviction:
the seven factors of enlightenment in the skin; the four truths in the bones;
compassion in the eyes and the blood; and a mind of loving-kindness in the black parts of the body.
The four bases of sympathy are known as his four feet;
the eight gates are the liberations, and the sixteen arms are the emptinesses.
The five Buddhas are his limbs, and he is wrathful for the sake of disciplining the wicked.
Purification by means of the three vajras brings about accomplishment through firmness of mind.
The lotuses have sixty-four, eight, sixteen, and thirty-two petals,
corresponding respectively to the nirmāṇa, dharma, saṃbhoga, and mahāsukha [bodies].
One should meditate upon the four wheels at the navel, heart, throat, and head,
which possess five rays and are white, black, red, and deep blue respectively.
Aṃ hūṃ oṃ haṃ; these are situated facing upward and downward as appropriate.
Through the purification of wisdom and means, they are declared to be in pairs.

Then, having drawn forth the assembly of the most excellent Victors dwelling in the triple world—perfected from beginningless time—by means of the multitudes of light rays from the seed-syllables at one's own heart, and having established them in the sky, one should worship them with the various distinctions of outer and secret offerings.

One should pray: "Oṃ, may the Vajra Tathāgatas consecrate me! Then, by those Tathāgatas who have assumed the form of Heruka, one is consecrated with five vases held in lotus hands, which contain the five nectars and possess the nature of the five Tathāgatas. While being consecrated, the Lord of the Mind (Akṣobhya) appears upon the head; there is a rain of flowers and also a rain of saffron. The sound of drums resounds. One is worshipped by Rūpavajrā and the others, and is praised by Locanā and the others with vajra songs.

Thereafter, having meditated upon one’s own consort (*svavidyā*), who has received empowerment through the eyes and other sense organs just like the Blessed One, one should perform the union of the five families (*pañcakulakalāpinī*) for the sake of further refinement. The sequence for this is as follows: at the head, heart, navel, secret place, and the pair of thighs, one should meditate on her limbs as being composed of atoms in the form of Vairocana, Akṣobhya, Ratnasaṃbhava, Amitābha, and Amoghasiddhi, produced from the seed-syllables Oṃ, Hūṃ, Svāhā, Āḥ, and Hā.

[The yogi] should visualize the pericarp of an eight-petaled lotus produced from the seed-syllables *hūṃ* and *āḥ*, and the excellent vajra-gem produced from *hūṃ* and *oṃ*. Having consecrated [the lotus and the gem] with the two mantras as appropriate: *Oṃ padma sukhādhāra mahārāgasukhaṃdada caturānandabhāg viśva hūṃ 3 kāryaṃ kuruṣva me.* *Oṃ vajra mahādveṣa caturānandadāyaka khagamukhaikaraso nātha hūṃ 3 kāryaṃ kuruṣva me.* He should then begin the act of passion (*rati*) together with her.
Thus is the samādhi named Ādiyoga.

Thereafter, having drawn in the wheel of Heruka with the goads of light rays from the seed-syllable in one’s own heart and caused him to enter into oneself, one should liquefy [the form] and emanate the host of Gaurī and the other Ḍākinīs from the Lord of the Maṇḍala, who is produced from the respective seed-syllables and signs generated by the lunar fluid fallen within the interior of the lotus. This is done with the mantra of emanation: *hūṃ aṃ gaṃ caṃ vaṃ ghaṃ puṃ śaṃ laṃ ḍaṃ*, and so forth.
Therein, one should cause the Blessed Lord—who is characterized by the arms, faces, colors, and other features as previously described—to enter into one’s own self together with the Blessed Lady.
One should meditate on Gaurī, who is black in color, holding a knife and a red lotus with her right and left hands, upon the sun at the seat of the eastern gate.
Likewise, one should meditate on Caurī, who is madder-red in color, playing a fire-drill (kṛpīṭa) and holding a boar, upon the seat of the southern gate;
and likewise Vettālī, who resembles molten gold, holding a tortoise and a lotus-vessel, upon the seat of the western gate.

Likewise, on the seat of the northern gate is Ghasmarī, resembling an emerald, holding a serpent and a yogic vessel; likewise, on the seat in the northeast corner is Pukkasi, resembling a sapphire, holding a lion and an axe;
and likewise, [on the seat of the northwest corner] is Śavarī, resembling the full moon, holding a mendicant’s bowl and a gourd.
In the same manner, one should meditate on Caṇḍālī, who is sky-blue in color and holds a wheel and a plow, seated upon the throne in the southeast corner;
likewise, one should meditate on Ḍombī, who is mottled in color and has hands in the *vajra* and *tarjanī* gestures, stationed upon the throne in the northwest corner.

All these Vajraḍākinīs stand in the dance posture with one leg half-crossed (*ardhaparyaṅka*), adorned with the five mudrās. Their hair is tawny and blazing upward, and they possess three round red eyes. They are resplendent with garlands of bloodless human heads and, being naked, they revel in the supreme bliss of the Lord.

Thus, when the maṇḍala circle has been completely perfected on all sides, one should gaze upon it. For the sake of attaining the knowledge of non-falling (acyutajñāna), through the yoga of the empowerment of the mudrās, one should contemplate a yellow syllable *phaṭ* at the aperture of the lotus-vajra.

Then, having seen the wisdom-maṇḍala drawn by the hook-like rays from the seed-syllable in the heart, facing the eastern gate, one should offer the guest-water (*argha*) and so forth, and perform the drawing in, entering, binding, and pleasing with these mantras: *Oṃ vajragaurī ākarṣaya jaḥ!* *Oṃ vajracaurī praveśaya hūṃ 2!* *Oṃ vajravettālī bandhaya vaṃ!* *Oṃ vajraghasmarī toṣaya hoḥ!* Thus, one should perform the drawing in, entering, binding, and pleasing.

Having contemplated the unification of the pledge (samaya) and the wisdom (jñāna) maṇḍalas, one should draw forth the assembly of the supreme Victors with rays from the seed-syllable in the heart, worship them, and entreat them for the sake of empowerment.

By means of those [waters], one is consecrated; from that consecration, the Consecration-Jinas arise upon the heads of those being consecrated. There, one should seal [them] with Citteśa, Buddharatneśa, and Vajradharmeśa, and with Gaurī, Caurī, Vettālī, and Ghasmarī in succession—these four goddesses beginning with Pukkasī, by these Buddhas respectively.

Then, having worshipped oneself—whose nature consists of the three realms and is the essence of the maṇḍala circle—with ḍākinīs emerging from the mouths of the light rays of the seed-syllable in the heart, their sprout-like hands offering various and manifold offerings, who are skilled in the perception of all things as being like an illusion and so forth, and with other external offerings specific to worship, one should perform a hymn of praise by means of collections of sounds resembling echoes, without forming a conceptual distinction between the object of worship, the worshipper, and the act of worship.
You are surrounded by a host of yoginīs; you are the one who has attained the supreme siddhi within your own mind.
By your compassionate heart, you have purified the entire world of moving and non-moving beings and awakened the seven [elements].
Having awakened the seven through the net of illusion (*māyā-pañca*), O proud Śrī Heruka, King of the Savaras, be pleased!

Then, in front [of the practitioner], there is a wind mandala arising from the syllable *yaṃ*, marked with a banner; above that, a fire mandala arising from the syllable *raṃ*, marked with flames; and above that, a lotus vessel born from the syllable *āḥ*. In its center are the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*) and the five lamps (*pañcapradīpa*), marked with the seed-syllables of the Tathāgatas. Through blazing and heating, impurities are drawn out, and it becomes like crystal. Above that is a vajra arising from the syllable *hūṃ*, empowered by all the Tathāgatas. Through cooking, it becomes liquefied and is empowered by the syllable *oṃ*. Then, having drawn in the wisdom-nectar (*jñānāmṛta*) of all the Tathāgatas via rays of light, one should make it of a single flavor (*samarasa*) right there.

One whose tongue is a *hūṃ*-vajra should satisfy [the deity] who is presided over by the three principles (*tritattva*), whose nature is incomparable taste, potency, and maturation, and upon whose heart-sun a mandala is placed.
By means of that, one should meditate on the Lord situated in the center of the circle of *ḍākinīs*. Such is the Lord. This is the samādhi called "The Supreme King of Mandalas."

Now, having emanated each one in sequence from Gaurī up to the Lord of the Maṇḍala of the Ḍākinīs throughout the ten directions, and having caused them to perform their respective teachings, one should dissolve them back into their proper places and behold the entire maṇḍala, with its task accomplished, as consisting of non-conceptual bliss.

Immediately thereafter, one should first meditate upon the syllable *Aṃ* of black color with rays of light in the *nirmāṇacakra*. Transformed into the form of a radiant drop (*bindu*), its rays emerge from every pore and illuminate the host of goddesses beginning with Gaurī, as well as the maṇḍala and the Lord of the Maṇḍala, who is intensely black like crushed collyrium, possessing a body that simultaneously flashes forth in the mode of emanation and withdrawal. In this very sequence, one should contemplate the six limbs: red in the second, yellow in the third, green in the fourth, blue in the fifth, and white in the sixth.

Afterwards, [the process] ending with the *virama* is again performed in the same manner. The eight *ḍākinīs*, beginning with Gaurī, have entered the eight directions facing their respective [deities]; they are to be meditated upon as having their own seed-syllables at their hearts.
Then, one should contemplate the Blessed Lady Nairātmyā having entered the heart of the Blessed One.

Thereupon, the Blessed One also, having emanated a mass of light rays from his four wheels, himself becoming composed of light rays, enters his own seed-syllable situated upon the sun within his heart. One should meditate on the sun as being within the seed-syllable, and the seed-syllable as being within the drop (*bindu*). That very drop, marked by the resonance (*nāda*) of the three and a half wheels, consisting of great bliss, and appearing in the form of a mass of white light rays, should be gradually dissolved into one's own self until it becomes unperceivable.
By this, it is shown that the universe itself, which is the very nature of one's own seed-consciousness, becomes of a single flavor in the form of great bliss.

If one becomes weary from meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*), one should recite the mantra. Having visualized the wheel—the self—manifested in the form of the deity, one should recite: *oṃ deva picu vajra hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā*. Alternatively, one may perform "vajra-recitation" (*vajrajāpa*) by mentally inscribing or observing the syllables of the root mantra established in the tantra, or the syllables of the heart-sun mantra, arranged in the shape of a mandala with their heads pointing upward and blazing, either through the mind alone or by mental visualization.

Or one may recite the words of wrath. One should utter the mantra from the eight mouths—the mouths of Gaurī and the other Ḍākinīs—and resolve upon it; this is the "recitation of the mass" (piṇḍajāpa).
When weary from recitation, one should make a formal vow.
May I be born into a noble family, free from madness, a holder of the commitments (*samayin*), and a teacher of Hevajra; may I be compassionate and devoted to the Guru in birth after birth.
May my hands ring the vajra and bell, and may I be a reciter of the profound Dharma.
May I become an absorber of the vital seed of women in birth after birth.

Then, having worshipped the maṇḍala-circle together with its presiding deities as before, one should internalize the host of ḍākinīs within the seed-syllable of one’s own heart; having resolved upon an exceedingly vast peaked pavilion, one should rise and dwell with a mind proud of the identity of the deity.

At the other two junctions [of the day] as well, one should sit in a place conducive to the mind and, as before, visualize the peaked pavilion (*kūṭāgāra*). In its center, one should instantly perceive oneself in the form of the Eight-Faced One, absorbed in the *nairātmyā* [meditation]. By the recitation of the three principles (*tritattva*), having seen [the deities] and having stationed the host of *ḍākinīs* emanated from their respective seed-syllables in their proper places, one should meditate on the entire mandala circle as consisting of great bliss (*mahāsukha*) and perform worship, praise, and so forth. At the time of sleep, one should fall asleep while bringing to mind the yoga of the cessation (*viramāntayoga*).
At the time of rising, one should rise up, exhorted by the songs of the four goddesses beginning with Pukkasī.
Having risen, one should act accordingly every day until the attainment of perfect awakening. This is the samādhi called Karmarājāgra.
If one lacks devotion to the sixteen-armed form, then within this very peaked pavilion (kūṭāgāra), one should visualize him as six-armed or four-armed.

Therein, the Blessed One is produced from his own emblem and seed-syllable; he is six-armed through the purification of the six perfections (ṣaṭpāramitā), and three-faced through the purification of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness (śūnyatā-animitta-apraṇihita). His body is blue like a lotus, the root face is blue, the left is red, and the right has the luster of the moon and dawn; he has three eyes and stands in the half-lotus posture (ardhaparyaṅka).

One should meditate upon her who has a vajra in her first right arm and a *kartṛ* (knife) in her second; a trident in her first left arm and a bell in her second; and with her remaining two arms, she is embraced by Vajraśṛṅkhalā. She tramples upon a corpse representing the three realms (*traidhātuka*).

One should visualize Vajraśṛṅkhalā as being blue in color, identical to Nairātmikā, adorned with various ornaments, holding a *kartṛ* and a skull-cup in her right and left hands respectively, and embracing the neck of her own lord with her vine-like arms. She has a single face.

In the same way, through the purity of having conquered the four Māras, he has four arms, resembles a blue lotus, and possesses three eyes. He stands upon a corpse in the half-lotus posture (*ardhaparyaṅka*). In his first right hand he holds a vajra; in his first left hand he holds a human skull-cup filled with the blood of gods and asuras. With his remaining two hands he embraces Vajravārāhī. The Blessed Lady is blue in color and holds a curved knife (*kartti*) and a skull-cup (*kapāla*) in her right and left hands respectively.
For these two, like the Causal Vajradhara and the Resultant [Vajradhara], one should specifically meditate upon their faces, hand-symbols, and so forth, as well as their moon-seats and moon-radiance;
for since the six-armed and four-armed forms lack eight faces, one should cause the host of ḍākinīs to enter the hair-pores of one's own body in their respective directions.
Oṃ kiṭi kiṭi vajra hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā. [This is] for the six-armed one.
Oṃ jvala jvala bhyo hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā. This is the mantra of the four-armed [deity].
The remainder is to be understood as before.
Written correctly at the command of the new Vajra of Passion, who has attained inconceivable gnosis, and not out of pride;
may the yogins forgive whatever faults have been written by me.
For the minds of the virtuous indeed take on the form of the autumnal moonbeams.
By whatever merit I have acquired through performing this Heruka sādhana,
may the entire world reach the further shore of the knowledge of the Omniscient One.
This is the work of the yogin, the illustrious Madanāṅgavajra.
